subsection: 4. Elements and principles of design in clothing

notes.b: The elements are the visual building blocks of a garment, and each can be changed to alter the look of the outfit.
points: Line: a visible edge or direction in a garment, created by seams, necklines, hemlines, trims, pleats and fastenings.
Shape: the outline of a garment or of an area within it, such as a neckline, sleeve or pocket.
Colour: hue, tone and intensity; warm colours such as red and orange advance, while cool colours such as blue and green recede.
Texture: the surface quality of a fabric, which can be smooth, rough, shiny or matt, and which can be seen or felt.
Pattern: the repetition of line, shape or colour over a surface, such as stripes, checks, herringbone, zig-zag or polka dots.

notes.h: Line and its effect on the figure
points: Vertical lines give the impression of length and make the figure look slimmer and taller.
Horizontal lines draw the eye across the body, which widens and shortens the figure.
Diagonal lines add contrast and movement, and they lead the eye across the garment.
Curved lines soften an outfit and add a feminine feel, such as the curve of a rounded neckline.
A princess seam, which runs from the shoulder or armhole to the hem, shapes the garment to the body without a waist seam.
Dark colours recede and reduce the apparent size of the figure, while light colours advance and enlarge it.
One colour worn from head to toe, or tonal shades of one colour, creates a longer, unbroken line.
Contrasting or complementary colours at the top and bottom divide the outfit and can balance the shape of the figure.
Shiny fabrics reflect light and increase the apparent size of the figure, while matt fabrics absorb light and reduce it.
Rough or heavily textured fabrics look bulkier, while smooth fabrics give a neater, more streamlined finish.
Small patterns suit small figures, and large patterns can be carried well by a larger figure.
Vertical stripes add height, and horizontal stripes add width and draw attention to the middle of the figure.
Pattern placed near the face or neckline draws attention to the upper body, which can distract from the lower body.
Narrow rectangular shapes slim the figure, while triangular shapes widen the top or bottom and balance the hips or shoulders.
A fitted bodice with a full skirt gives an hourglass shape, and a fitted top with straight trousers gives a streamlined shape.

notes.b: The principles describe how the elements are arranged to create a unified garment.
points: Proportion: the relationship between the sizes of parts of a garment, such as pockets sized to the garment and a collar sized to the neckline.
Balance: the way the parts of a design are distributed, which may be symmetrical, asymmetrical or vertical.
Emphasis: a focal point that draws the eye to one area over another, created by a brooch, contrasting trim, a bold hemline or a neckline.
Harmony: the sense that all parts of a design work together and complement one another, for example by repeating one colour.
Rhythm or repetition: the repeated use of a colour, line or shape, which moves the eye through the garment.

notes.h: Applying the elements and principles to garment construction
points: Seams join the parts of a garment, and their placement creates line and can add shaping to the body.
Darts remove excess fabric to shape a garment around the bust, waist or hips.
Pleats and gathers add fullness and movement to a skirt or sleeve, and they can add visual interest at the waist.
Pockets, fastenings and collars add line and emphasis, and they must be positioned in proportion to the garment.
Fabric choice affects how the design hangs, whether a crisp shape holds or a soft drape flows.

notes.b: A garment is evaluated against three criteria: how well its design serves its function, its comfort and its aesthetic appeal.
points: Function: the garment must suit the activity, climate and occasion it is intended for, such as freedom of movement for sport.
Comfort: the fabric, fit and ease of movement determine whether the wearer is comfortable.
Aesthetic appeal: the colour, line, texture and proportion must produce an attractive and pleasing overall look.
A well-designed garment shows a clear relationship between the design features and the function they serve.
Using colour and design to flatter the body: choose colours and lines that emphasise the wearer's best features and balance any areas they wish to de-emphasise.

keyTerms.definition: The basic visual components of a garment: line, shape, colour, texture and pattern.
The ways in which the elements are arranged, including proportion, balance, emphasis, harmony and rhythm.
The relationship between the size of one part of a garment and the size of another part or of the whole.
The creation of a focal point that draws the eye to one area of a garment.
The sense that all the parts of a design work together and complement each other.
The movement of the eye through a garment created by the repetition of a colour, line or shape.
A stitched fold of fabric that removes excess material to shape a garment around a body curve.
A long seam running from the shoulder or armhole to the hem that shapes a garment without a waist seam.

factCards.definition: Line, shape, colour, texture and pattern.

factCards.term: Three effects of vertical lines on the figure
factCards.definition: They give the impression of length, make the figure look slimmer and taller, and draw the eye upward.

factCards.term: Two effects of light colours on the figure
factCards.definition: They advance and enlarge the figure, making it look bigger.

factCards.term: Three criteria for evaluating a garment

factCards.definition: They add width to the figure and draw attention to the middle of the body.

factCards.term: Two functions of darts and pleats in construction
factCards.definition: Darts remove excess fabric to create shape around the body, and pleats add fullness and movement to a skirt or sleeve.

factCards.term: Three ways to achieve balance in a design
factCards.definition: Symmetrical, asymmetrical and vertical balance, each of which distributes the parts of a design differently.

questions.prompt: Name three elements of design and state how one of them can be used to make a short figure look taller.
questions.model: Three elements: line, colour and texture. Line can make a short figure look taller by using vertical lines, such as a long open jacket, a princess seam or a column of buttons, which give an impression of length. Dark, matt colours in the outfit can also help the figure look longer, because they recede and reduce the visual size of the body.

questions.prompt: Explain how the principles of emphasis and proportion can be applied to the design of an outfit for a formal occasion.
questions.model: Emphasis: a focal point such as an embellished neckline, a contrasting brooch or a bold hemline draws the eye to one feature, and the rest of the outfit is kept simpler so that the focal point stands out. Proportion: the sizes of the parts are in balance with each other and with the wearer, for example a single colour running from neckline to hem creates an unbroken line, and pockets, collars and trims are sized to suit the garment. A well-proportioned outfit looks harmonious and suits the occasion.
